candidate_sources.title: Collar Rot and Alternaria Stem Canker of Tomato
candidate_sources.snippet: Dark brown to black cankers with concentric zonation occur on stems near the soil line or aboveground. Cankers enlarge, girdle the stem before harvest, and kill the plants. Alternaria stem canker is caused by A. alternata f. sp. lycopersici and is primarily a problem of coastal-grown tomatoes in California. Fungicides that control black mold are effective against Alternaria stem canker.

candidate_sources.title: Alternaria Stem Canker / Tomato / Agriculture: Pest Management Guidelines / UC Statewide IPM Program
candidate_sources.snippet: Alternaria stem canker symptoms include dark brown sunken lesions with characteristic concentric rings develop on green fruit either on plants or during postharvest transit of ripening fruit. Vascular tissue about 2 inches above and below the cankers exhibit brown streaks. Humid climates and semiarid climates with frequent dews that provide high moisture (≥ 90% relative humidity) are conducive for disease development.

candidate_sources.title: Alternaria Canker - Vegetable Resources / Texas A&M AgriLife Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Alternaria canker causes dark brown to black areas of dead tissue between leaf veins caused by a toxin produced by the fungus. Many tomato cultivars with high levels of resistance to Alternaria stem canker are available. Disease management includes cultural practices, resistant varieties, and fungicide applications for control.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose of Tomato | Oklahoma State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Detailed extension factsheet covering symptoms (circular lesions on ripe fruit with concentric rings), causal pathogen (Colletotrichum species), disease conditions (warm, wet weather), and management strategies including resistant varieties and fungicide options.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato: Anthracnose (Ripe Rot) - Integrated Pest Management
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Connecticut IPM factsheet on tomato anthracnose (ripe rot), describing symptoms on ripening fruit, pathogen biology, disease cycle, and integrated management recommendations including cultural practices and fungicide applications.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato: Anthracnose | Hortsense | Washington State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Washington State University Hortsense factsheet on tomato anthracnose with comprehensive coverage of symptoms, pathogen (Colletotrichum), optimal conditions for disease development (80°F with moisture), and management approaches.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial canker of tomato | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Caused by the seedborne pathogen Clavibacter michiganensis subspecies michiganensis. The pathogen systemically colonizes tomato xylem leading to unilateral leaflet wilt, marginal leaf necrosis, stem and petiole cankers, and plant death.

candidate_sources.title: Clavibacter michiganensis (bacterial canker of tomato) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Gram-positive actinobacterium causing bacterial canker of tomato with worldwide distribution. Seedborne pathogen systemically colonizes tomato xylem leading to unilateral leaflet wilt, marginal leaf necrosis, stem and petiole cankers, and plant death. Splash dispersal of bacterium onto fruit exteriors causes bird's-eye lesions.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Canker of Tomato: Revisiting a Global and Economically Damaging Seedborne Pathogen | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Gram-positive actinobacterium Clavibacter michiganensis causes bacterial canker of tomato, an economically impactful disease with worldwide distribution. This seedborne pathogen systemically colonizes tomato xylem leading to unilateral leaflet wilt, marginal leaf necrosis, stem and petiole cankers, and plant death.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Canker | Cornell Vegetables
candidate_sources.snippet: Caused by Clavibacter michiganensis subspecies michiganensis. Lower leaves wilt, often on one side. Entire plant may collapse and die. Fruit displays small raised white spots with tan or brown centers (bird's eye spot). Brown streaks visible in vascular system when stem is cut open.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Speck of Tomato – Wisconsin Horticulture
candidate_sources.snippet: Small black spots (⅛ to ¼ inch diameter) on leaves with yellow halos; fruit spots very small, pinpoint-like, not penetrating deep tissue. Caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato. Transmitted via contaminated seed and transplants; favors cool (63-75°F) wet weather. Management: use drip irrigation, avoid working with wet plants, sanitize tools with bleach or 70% alcohol.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Speck | Cornell Vegetables
candidate_sources.snippet: Dedicated factsheet on bacterial speck of tomato covering symptom identification on foliage and fruit, disease etiology caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato, conditions favoring disease development, and integrated pest management strategies including cultural, chemical, and varietal resistance approaches.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Speck of Tomato | Vegetable Disease Facts - Ohio State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Ohio State University extension resource providing comprehensive information on bacterial speck of tomato, including symptom description, pathogen identification (Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato), disease cycle, environmental conditions promoting infection, and management recommendations for vegetable growers.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Wilt of Tomato | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial wilt is a serious disease caused by Ralstonia solanacearum. Symptoms include wilting of youngest leaves while plants remain green, brown discoloration of vascular tissue in stem cross-sections, and root rot at the plant base. The disease develops rapidly in warm, wet conditions and can cause plant death within 2-3 weeks.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Wilt of Tomatoes | Oklahoma State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Southern bacterial wilt (also called bacterial wilt) of tomato is caused by the soil-borne bacterium Ralstonia solanacearum. The pathogen enters through root wounds from transplanting, cultivation, and insect feeding. Management includes use of resistant varieties, sanitation of tools and equipment, and avoiding overhead irrigation.

candidate_sources.title: Southern Bacterial Wilt of Tomato Found | University of Maryland Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Southern bacterial wilt of tomato, caused by Ralstonia solanacearum, is an economically important disease in warm climates. Affected plants show wilting despite adequate moisture, yellowing of lower leaves, and brown discoloration of vascular bundles. The bacterium survives in soil and infected plant debris.

candidate_sources.title: Understanding and Managing Cucumber Mosaic Virus
candidate_sources.snippet: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) is a widespread plant virus with a host range exceeding 1,200 species. Symptoms on tomato include filiformity (thin, shoestring-like leaves), yellowing, mottling, stunting, and bushy growth. Infected plants produce fewer marketable fruit, with remaining fruit small, mottled, or necrotic. Transmission occurs through aphids (stylet-borne), mechanical sap contact, seeds, and dodder parasitic weeds.

candidate_sources.title: Vegetable: Cucumber Mosaic Virus - UMass Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Cucumber Mosaic Virus causes severe crop losses across diverse plant species. On vegetables including tomato, symptoms manifest as leaf mottling, yellowing, distortion, and plant stunting. The virus is transmitted by multiple aphid species in a non-persistent manner, making management through vector control and resistant varieties critical for disease prevention.

candidate_sources.title: Cucumber Mosaic Virus - Penn State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) is a widely distributed pathogenic virus in the family Bromoviridae with the broadest host range of any known plant virus. Symptoms include mosaic patterns, leaf deformation, stunting, and reduced fruit quality. Management strategies include use of resistant cultivars, control of aphid vectors, removal of infected plants, and sanitation practices.

candidate_sources.title: Mosaic Virus Diseases Caused by Cucumoviruses / Tomato - UC IPM Program
candidate_sources.snippet: Cucumovirus-caused mosaic diseases on tomato result in mottled, distorted foliage and significant yield reductions. Cucumber Mosaic Virus, a member of the Cucumovirus genus, is transmitted by aphids in a non-persistent manner. Integrated pest management includes identifying symptoms early, controlling aphid populations, planting resistant varieties, and eliminating host weeds and volunteer plants.

candidate_sources.title: Early Blight of Tomato | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Early blight is a common disease of tomato caused by the fungus Alternaria linariae. The main symptom is round leaf spots with a characteristic target appearance due to dark concentric rings. Disease develops at moderate to warm temperatures (59-80°F, optimum 82-86°F) with wet weather or high relative humidity.

candidate_sources.title: Early blight in tomato and potato | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Early blight affects both tomato and potato crops. Caused by Alternaria species fungi, it produces characteristic target-shaped lesions with concentric rings on leaves, stems, and fruit. Management includes cultural practices and fungicide applications during conditions favorable for disease development.

candidate_sources.title: Early Blight of Tomatoes | University of Maryland Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Early blight is a fungal disease of tomato leaves and stems. Lesions appear first on lower, older leaves with characteristic bull's-eye patterns caused by concentric rings of alternating dark and light colored tissue. The disease is favored by moderate temperatures and wet conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Botrytis Gray Mold of Tomato | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Tomato leaf and stem lesions are tan to brown in color. Symptoms include light tan or brownish v-shaped spots on the leaves, beginning at their margins. Later, fluffy gray spores cover the surface of the spots. Stem infections occur through leaf scars, cracks, and pruning wounds. Botrytis produces a dense velvety gray brown spore mass on infected tissue which when disturbed releases a cloud of spores. Gray mold is most virulent when the environment is cool (60-70° F) and the relative humidity is high (≥ 80%).

candidate_sources.title: Gray mold of tomatoes | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Gray mold is caused by the fungus Botrytis cinerea. The disease affects leaves, stems, flowers and fruit of tomato plants. Leaf lesions are light tan or brown and develop v-shaped spots starting at leaf margins. Management requires preventive fungicide applications, pruning to reduce humidity, and proper sanitation practices.

candidate_sources.title: Botrytis cinerea (grey mould-rot) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Botrytis cinerea causes grey mould disease affecting over 200 host species. The etiological agent is an asexual fungus. CABI datasheet covers identity, distribution, diagnosis, biology & ecology, environmental requirements, natural enemies, impacts, and control strategies. No known resistant tomato cultivars exist; fungicide rotation and preventive applications are essential for management.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato Late Blight | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Late blight is caused by the pathogen Phytophthora infestans. Symptoms on tomato leaves are irregularly shaped, water-soaked lesions with lighter halos. On fruit, greenish-brown greasy-appearing spots develop. The disease is favored by cool, wet weather with nights in the 50s-60s and rainy conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Late blight of tomato and potato | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Late blight caused by Phytophthora infestans affects both tomato and potato. On tomato leaves, lesions appear water-soaked with a lighter halo, often showing white cottony growth indicating spore production. Management includes fungicide applications, resistant varieties, and sanitation practices. The pathogen spreads rapidly in cool, moist conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato Late Blight - UW Vegetable Pathology
candidate_sources.snippet: Tomato late blight is caused by the oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans. Initial symptoms are irregularly shaped, water-soaked lesions on younger leaves in the upper canopy, followed by white cottony growth from spore production. Environmental conditions favoring infection include cool nights and wet days.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato leaf mold | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Discrete yellow spots on the upper side of the leaf and olive-green to brown velvety mold on the underside are characteristic. Caused by Passalora fulva (formerly Cladosporium fulvum). Optimal temperature 71-75°F with high humidity (>85%) favoring disease. Management includes removing infected leaves, improving air circulation, reducing nitrogen fertilizer, and using resistant varieties.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato Leaf Mold | Cornell Vegetables
candidate_sources.snippet: Fungal disease caused by Passalora fulva affecting greenhouse and high-tunnel tomatoes. Symptoms include pale greenish-yellow spots (<1/4 inch) on upper leaf surfaces with olive-green velvety spores on lower surface. New spores form within 10-12 days under humid conditions. Management through cultural practices, fungicide applications, and resistant cultivar selection.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato Leaf Mold Diseases | Purdue University Vegetable Crops Hotline
candidate_sources.snippet: Leaf mold caused by Passalora fulva is common in Indiana high tunnels. Optimum temperature 71-75°F with chlorotic (bright yellow) lesions on upper leaf surface. Cercospora leaf mold (Pseudocercospora fuligena) is alternative with mustard-yellow lesions, optimal temp 82°F. Management includes sanitation, crop rotation, resistant varieties, and fungicides (mancozeb, Inspire Super®, Tanos®, Quadris Top®).

candidate_sources.title: Late blight of potato and tomato | APS Education Center
candidate_sources.snippet: Phytophthora infestans is an oomycete (water mold) that causes late blight on tomato and potato. The pathogen produces sporangia that spread via wind and water splash. Characteristic symptoms include water-soaked spots with concentric rings on leaves and stems, and soft rot on tubers and fruits. Environmental conditions favoring disease: cool temperatures (60-70°F), high humidity, and free water on plant surfaces.

candidate_sources.title: LEAF MOLD AND POWDERY MILDEW OF TOMATO
candidate_sources.snippet: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station factsheet covering symptoms including white superficial mycelium on leaves and stems, yellowing, desiccation, necrosis and defoliation. Details pathogen species including Oidium neolycopersici, Leveillula taurica, and Erysiphe species. Provides management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Vegetable: Solanaceous, Powdery Mildew - UMass Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: UMass Extension factsheet on powdery mildew of solanaceous crops (tomato, pepper, eggplant). Covers symptom development with light green to bright yellow spots progressing to white powdery appearance, pathogen identification, and integrated management strategies for vegetable growers.

candidate_sources.title: Powdery Mildew on Field-Grown Tomatoes - UC Statewide IPM Program
candidate_sources.snippet: UC Davis Integrated Pest Management program guide for field-grown tomato powdery mildew. Provides detailed information on symptom recognition, pathogen biology, disease development, and environmental conditions favoring infection. Emphasizes practical management approaches for California growers.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizopus Rot - Plant Pathology - University of Florida
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizopus rot appears water-soaked and may exude a clear liquid. A characteristic symptom of rhizopus rot is water soaked regions on the fruit leading to puffy white growth that collapses the outer fruit tissue, with white fungal mycelia and large masses of black mustard-like spores on raised stalks.

candidate_sources.title: HS866/HS131: Guide to Identifying and Controlling Postharvest Tomato Diseases in Florida
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Florida IFAS Extension guide to identifying and controlling postharvest tomato diseases, including fungal diseases such as Rhizopus soft rot. Covers disease identification, symptoms, pathogen biology, and management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato rot by Rhizopus microsporus alters native fungal community composition and secondary metabolite production
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed research on tomato rot caused by Rhizopus microsporus, examining pathogen biology, symptom development, and impacts on fruit microbiota and metabolite production.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizopus stolonifer Exhibits Necrotrophic Behavior when Causing Soft Rot in Ripe Fruit
candidate_sources.snippet: American Phytopathological Society (APS) publication detailing R. stolonifer's necrotrophic behavior mechanism when causing soft rot in ripe fruit, including pathogen biology and host-pathogen interactions on tomato and other hosts.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizopus | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on Rhizopus genus covering identity, distribution, hosts affected (including tomato), diagnosis, prevention and control strategies for Rhizopus soft rot diseases.

candidate_sources.title: Timber Rot on Tomato - Missouri Produce Growers Bulletin, University of Missouri IPM
candidate_sources.snippet: Timber rot of tomato, also called sclerotinia stem rot, is caused by Sclerotinia sclerotiorum. Initial symptoms appear as water-soaked areas on stems at or above soil level. White fuzzy mold develops, followed by bleaching and blackening of tissues. Black sclerotia (fungal bodies) form within 7-10 days. Disease is encouraged by cool, wet conditions and high humidity.

candidate_sources.title: Frequently Asked Questions About Timber Rot on Tomato - Penn State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Timber rot on tomatoes is caused by Sclerotinia sclerotiorum. Symptoms include water-soaked lesions on stems and leaf axils, wilting, plant collapse, and white mold growth. Black sclerotia develop inside and on affected tissue. The pathogen survives in soil for up to 10 years. Management includes reducing humidity, improving drainage, and removing infected plant material.

candidate_sources.title: Integrated Disease Management of Timber Rot of Tomatoes - LSU Agricultural Center
candidate_sources.snippet: Timber rot, caused by Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, is a serious fungal disease of tomatoes. Symptoms appear as water-soaked lesions at stem nodes and axils, with white mycelial growth and development of black sclerotia. Disease management requires integrated approaches including cultural practices, environmental control, chemical fungicides, and biological controls.

candidate_sources.title: Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Circular, tan to gray lesions develop on the lower leaves and stems of the plant. Lesions typically contain small dark spots (pycnidia) where spores are produced. Disease is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. Optimal conditions are warm, wet weather with temperatures between 68-77°F.

candidate_sources.title: Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomatoes | University of Maryland Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms start on lower leaves and progress upward. Lesions are small and circular with dark-brown borders and yellow halos. The pathogen Septoria lycopersici overwinters on infected debris and spreads via rain splash. Most problematic in humid conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Septoria Leaf Spot | Extension | West Virginia University
candidate_sources.snippet: Fungal disease caused by Septoria lycopersici affecting tomato foliage. Characteristic small circular lesions with gray centers and dark margins appear on lower leaves first. Disease management includes removing infected leaves and improving air circulation.

candidate_sources.title: Ralstonia solanacearum (bacterial wilt of potato) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI datasheet covering Identity, Overview, Associated Diseases, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts/Species Affected, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Environmental Requirements, and Prevention/Control for Ralstonia solanacearum, which causes bacterial wilt affecting over 250 plant species including tomato.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Wilt - Ralstonia solanacearum | Penn State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Penn State extension publication on bacterial wilt caused by Ralstonia solanacearum. Covers symptoms, diagnosis, disease development in high temperatures and moist soils, and management strategies including crop rotation, resistant rootstocks, and elimination of weeds.

candidate_sources.title: Organic Management of Bacterial Wilt of Tomato and Potato Caused by Ralstonia solanacearum | eOrganic
candidate_sources.snippet: eOrganic guide on organic management strategies for bacterial wilt of tomato caused by Ralstonia solanacearum. Covers cultural practices, crop rotation, resistant varieties, and alternative management approaches for organic production systems.

candidate_sources.title: Southern Blight of Tomato | Oklahoma State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Southern blight is caused by Sclerotinia rolfsii. The initial symptoms are rapid wilting of the entire plant. A water-soaked lesion on the stem near the soil line rapidly expands, turns brown, and girdles the stem. A white mold (mycelium) eventually covers the stem lesion. Small, uniformly round sclerotia (about 1/16 inch diameter) form on the mycelium, first white then becoming brown, resembling mustard seeds.

candidate_sources.title: Southern Blight – Wisconsin Horticulture
candidate_sources.snippet: Southern blight disease of vegetables is caused by the fungus Sclerotinia rolfsii. The disease is favored by high humidity and soil moisture with warm to hot temperatures (85-95°F). The fungus survives in the soil as sclerotia which may build to high numbers when susceptible plants are cropped repeatedly. Crop rotation with non-susceptible grass crops such as corn is the most effective management strategy.

candidate_sources.title: Diagnosing Southern Blight and White Mold in Tomato and Pepper — Plant & Pest Advisory
candidate_sources.snippet: Rutgers University diagnostic guide for distinguishing Southern Blight (Sclerotinia rolfsii) from White Mold in tomato and pepper crops. Covers symptom recognition, pathogen identification, environmental conditions favoring disease development, and integrated management approaches for commercial and home gardeners.

candidate_sources.title: Target Spot of Tomato in Florida
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive extension factsheet covering target spot disease caused by Corynespora cassiicola, including symptoms (pinpoint-sized water-soaked spots developing into necrotic lesions with light brown centers and dark margins), environmental conditions (83-90°F with high humidity, requires 16-44 hours leaf wetness), and integrated management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Target Spot of Tomato
candidate_sources.snippet: Industry agronomic resource providing detailed information on Target Spot disease symptoms, identification characteristics, and disease management recommendations for tomato growers.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato Diseases & Disorders
candidate_sources.snippet: University extension guide covering multiple tomato diseases including Target Spot, with symptom descriptions and management strategies as part of comprehensive tomato disease identification resource.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus on Tomato and Pepper | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: NC State Extension publication covering TSWV symptoms on tomatoes and peppers including bronzed uppermost leaves with small brown lesions, fruit with chlorotic ring spots and deformation. Discusses thrips transmission vectors.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus - USU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Utah State University Extension IPM note dedicated to Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus covering identification, pathogen biology, and integrated pest management strategies for vegetable crops.

candidate_sources.title: Tomato Spotted Wilt / Tomato / Agriculture: Pest Management Guidelines / UC Statewide IPM Program
candidate_sources.snippet: UC Davis Statewide IPM Program page providing comprehensive pest management guidelines for tomato spotted wilt in tomato production, including cultural and chemical management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Verticillium Wilt of Tomato and Eggplant | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet covering symptoms including yellowing of lower leaves, V-shaped lesions, wilting, and brown necrotic tissue development. Details on pathogen Verticillium albo-atrum and V. dahliae, survival in soil via microsclerotia for up to 10 years, and management strategies including resistant varieties, crop rotation (4-5 years), sanitation, and soil solarization.

candidate_sources.title: Verticillium dahliae (verticillium wilt) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Digital Library datasheet providing comprehensive information on Verticillium dahliae including identity, distribution, dispersal, host range, diagnosis, biology and ecology, natural enemies, and integrated management strategies. Covers vascular discoloration symptoms and methods to distinguish from Fusarium wilt.

candidate_sources.title: Solanaceous, Verticillium Wilt - UMass Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet focused on Verticillium wilt of solanaceous crops including tomato. Documents symptom progression from chlorotic and necrotic lower foliage, management through resistant varieties, crop rotation with non-host plants, sanitation of infected plant material, and soil heating to control soil-borne fungal structures.
